name: Tripterygium hypoglaucum
short: Honey poisoning the plant appears to cause: 31 cases, 8 deaths (China). Tablets in 30 transplant patients: periods disrupted in 73% of women, sperm fell in men (reversible). A review flags liver harm.
text: Tripterygium hypoglaucum belongs to the same genus as thunder god vine (Tripterygium wilfordii), which has its own entry; a 2021 review describes it as a medicine with both significant efficacy and potential toxicity, with reports of liver, kidney and genital-system toxicity, and says its side effects are the key limitation on its clinical use. The review adds that its potential for serious liver problems has received particular attention in recent years. A 2013 meta-analysis of 75 randomised trials (4,386 participants) of Tripterygium preparations for chronic kidney disease pooled Tripterygium glycoside tablets, Tripterygium hypoglaucum tablets and Tripterygium granules or extracts; the abstract does not give results for each preparation. Compared with placebo, standard care or other immunosuppressive treatment, the pooled preparations increased the rate of abnormal liver function test results (relative risk 4.03) and of altered menstruation (relative risk 5.29); the authors note suboptimal study quality. Its most serious reported harm comes from honey: in a case series of 31 honey poisonings in southwest China (2007 to 2012), all after eating at least 100 g of honey, 8 people died (25.8%); severe cases developed little or no urine output, twitching, blood in the urine, bruising or bloody stools, and Tripterygium hypoglaucum pollen was found in 22 of 29 honey samples; the authors say the plant appears to be the cause. Taken as tablets: in a 6-month single-group study of 30 kidney-transplant recipients with proteinuria given a tablet extract by mouth, the main adverse effect was reversible toxicity to the reproductive organs; menstrual irregularities affected 73.3% of the 15 women at 6 months, with raised FSH and LH and lower estradiol and progesterone, and sperm concentration and viability fell markedly in the 15 men, while kidney function, liver enzymes and blood counts did not change significantly. In 13 men with rheumatoid arthritis taking it by mouth, sperm concentration and motility were significantly lower than in 11 untreated men; hormone levels did not change and the effect appeared reversible. In a 4-week placebo-controlled trial of the tablets with cetirizine in 78 adults with chronic urticaria, the stated aim included safety, but the abstract reports no adverse-event results. Interactions: in a rat study, a tablet made from a water extract of the peeled root of Tripterygium hypoglaucum, given by mouth, significantly raised blood levels of tacrolimus given by mouth, in a dose- and time-dependent way, but did not change tacrolimus given into a vein. Tacrolimus is a medicine the study describes as widely used in kidney diseases. These are animal data; no human interaction data were found in the cited sources.
